summary.title: ClawKeeper: Comprehensive Safety Protection for OpenClaw Agents Through Skills, Plugins, and Watchers

details: Open-source autonomous agent runtimes (OpenClaw-style) hold broad privileges (shell, local files, messaging apps), turning model errors into system-level threats; existing defenses are fragmented point solutions that are static, reactive, and tightly coupled to the agent, forcing a safety-utility tradeoff.

ClawKeeper: a three-layer real-time safety framework combining (1) skill-level injected security policies in the agent context, (2) an in-runtime plugin enforcing hardening, threat detection, config integrity and behavioral logging/scanning, and (3) a Watcher.

Key design principle: the Watcher is a structurally decoupled second agent instance that receives streamed live session state/tool calls over a WebSocket and can halt execution or force human confirmation, giving regulatory separation of safety from task solving, tamper resistance, and independent self-evolution of safety knowledge.

Skill layer: security rules as Markdown documents plus scripts; system-level constraints for Windows (not Linux-only) and software-level constraints exemplified with Feishu/Lark; scheduled (cron) security scans and interaction-summary auditing; can be distilled to pure prompts injected into AGENTS.md.

Plugin layer: OWASP Agentic Security / CVE-aligned threat detection (exposed gateway ports, weak permissions, plaintext credentials), hardening (bind gateway to 127.0.0.1, inject safety rules into AGENTS.md), cryptographic hash backups of openclaw.json / AGENTS.md / SOUL.md, full-lifecycle logging plus asynchronous behavioral log scanning.

Watcher layer: separate OpenClaw instance with monitoring skills/plugins, installed via a Markdown config that triggers a safe hot-restart of the task agent; decisions include ask_user, stop, tool_loop_limit interruption; supports local (privacy, file/skill scanning) and cloud (one Watcher supervising many instances) deployment.
140 adversarial instances: 7 threat categories x 20 cases (10 simple, 10 complex).

Categories: prompt injection, credential/sensitive data leakage, privilege escalation & tampering, dangerous command execution, config file tampering, vulnerability/threat detection (OWASP ASI-aligned), malicious skill installation.
Metric: Defense Success Rate, judged by two independent human annotators on execution traces following the Agent-SafetyBench protocol.
Seven open-source OpenClaw security repositories: OpenGuardrails, ClawSec, OSPG, SecureClaw, OpenClaw Shield, ClawBands, Clawscan-Skills; unsupported task categories marked as '-'.
Clean OpenClaw installation (version 2026.3.8) with GLM-5 as the underlying LLM for all methods; qualitative case studies on Windows with Feishu (Lark) integration.

Qualitative case studies per layer (Base64-obfuscated payload blocking, credential redaction before/after plugin install, threat-detection report with security score 83/100 and auto-fix, behavioral scan over 228 logged events detecting a jailbreak, Watcher interventions on dangerous commands, tool-loop limits, and retry-after-failure loops).
Comparative qualitative rating of the three paradigms on safety, compatibility, flexibility, running cost, deployment difficulty.
Simulated online-learning experiment on Watcher self-evolution over 1-100 unseen adversarial cases.

key_findings.finding: The unified three-layer framework achieves substantially higher defense success than any single existing open-source defense across all threat categories.
key_findings.evidence: On the 140-instance benchmark with GLM-5, ClawKeeper reaches 85-90% DSR on all seven categories versus 45-70% for baselines within their supported categories, a margin of 15-45 percentage points over the best baseline per category.

key_findings.finding: Existing OpenClaw defenses are severely fragmented in coverage, not just weaker in accuracy.
key_findings.evidence: No baseline supports more than three of the seven task categories (e.g., OpenClaw Shield covers only privilege monitoring T3, Clawscan-Skills only malicious skills T7, OpenGuardrails only two), while ClawKeeper covers all seven; feature tables similarly show every skill/plugin baseline missing at least one of the four/five key functionalities.

key_findings.finding: A decoupled external Watcher agent is the strongest and most generalizable paradigm, since it cannot be uninstalled by task-level instructions and separates safety from task objectives.
key_findings.evidence: Comparative analysis rates watcher-based highest on safety, compatibility, and flexibility (versus low safety for skill-based and low compatibility/flexibility for plugin-based); qualitative cases show the Watcher overriding the task agent with ask_user on a decoded Base64 destructive command, interrupting on tool_loop_limit, and issuing stop after an upstream permission failure with a retry-loop instruction.

key_findings.finding: The Watcher can self-evolve its safety coverage from operational experience, unlike static skill or plugin rules.
key_findings.evidence: In a simulated online setting, Watcher DSR rises from about 90% to about 95% over 100 previously unseen adversarial cases, attributed to updated monitoring skills/in-context memory and recalibrated confirmation thresholds, while skill- and plugin-based paradigms show flat trajectories.

key_findings.finding: Plugin-level hardening that injects risk-awareness rules into the agent's core configuration measurably changes runtime behavior on sensitive data.
key_findings.evidence: Before/after case study: the un-hardened agent printed plaintext GitHub credentials from a summarized local file, whereas after hardening (rules injected into AGENTS.md) the agent returned the legitimate notes with credentials replaced by a policy notice.
